ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Expels Sudanese Diplomats Amid Regional Tensions | Kulu Media Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Connect with us Search Kulu Media Ethiopia Orders Six Sudanese Diplomats to Leave as Regional Tensions Escalate Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Home » News » Ethiopia » Ethiopia Orders Six Sudanese Diplomats to Leave as Regional Tensions Escalate Ethiopia Ethiopia Orders Six Sudanese Diplomats to Leave as Regional Tensions Escalate Six Sudanese consular staff ordered out as Ethiopia-Sudan tensions deepen. Published 58 seconds ago on November 4, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed (left) and Sudanese military leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan (right), pictured in a composite image as diplomatic tensions between the two countries escalate. Image: Kulu Media (Illustration) Ethiopia has ordered six Sudanese consular staff members to leave the country within 48 hours, deepening a diplomatic dispute between the neighboring countries amid allegations involving Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia. A senior Ethiopian official confirmed the departure order to Reuters in a report published on November 4, 2026. The six officials were stationed at Sudan’s consulate in Assosa, the capital of Ethiopia’s Benishangul-Gumuz region near the Sudanese border. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, did not explain the reason for the decision. Ethiopia’s government had not publicly provided a detailed explanation of the move at the time of the Reuters report. The expulsion order comes amid worsening relations between Addis Ababa and Khartoum, with both governments accusing each other of involvement in armed conflicts affecting the wider Horn of Africa. Sudan has accused Ethiopia of allowing the RSF to use Ethiopian territory to launch drone attacks against civilian infrastructure inside Sudan. Khartoum says it has submitted complaints to the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council over the alleged attacks. The latest accusations follow months of Ethiopia-Sudan tensions involving border security, drone operations and the wider Sudanese civil war. Sudanese military officials have previously alleged that RSF drones were being launched from Ethiopian territory, claims rejected by Addis Ababa. Ethiopia denies supporting the RSF. The allegations concerning the use of Ethiopian territory for drone operations have not been independently established. The diplomatic dispute has intensified as Sudan’s civil war continues and renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises concerns about the security of the region’s shared borders. Ethiopia, meanwhile, has accused neighboring countries of supporting TPLF-aligned forces involved in renewed hostilities against the Ethiopian federal government. The accusations specifically concern Sudan, Eritrea and Egypt, all of which have denied supporting the armed groups. The competing allegations have heightened tensions between governments already facing significant security and diplomatic challenges. Assosa’s location gives the latest development particular significance. The town lies in western Ethiopia, close to Sudan, and serves as an important administrative center in a region affected by cross-border security concerns. Sudan’s consular presence there has provided a channel for official communication and assistance to Sudanese nationals. The departure of the six staff members could further complicate diplomatic engagement, although the immediate consequences for consular services remain unclear. The latest development follows a series of diplomatic confrontations involving Ethiopia and neighboring countries. On October 1, Ethiopia ordered the closure of its embassy in Eritrea and expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats, accusing Asmara of activities threatening Ethiopian national security. Eritrea subsequently announced that it was severing diplomatic relations with Ethiopia, while the two governments exchanged accusations over the renewed conflict in northern Ethiopia. The deterioration in relations coincided with reports of Eritrean military movements inside eastern Tigray and drone strikes reportedly targeting Eritrean forces. The reported incidents further increased concerns about a wider regional confrontation. The diplomatic dispute also extended to Egypt after Addis Ababa ordered an Egyptian diplomat to leave the country and Cairo responded with a reciprocal measure. The African Union called for restraint and urged the governments involved to resolve their differences through diplomatic channels. The growing tensions have renewed concerns that separate conflicts in Ethiopia and Sudan could become increasingly interconnected. Sudan’s civil war began in April 2023 following a power struggle between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF. The conflict has caused widespread destruction, mass displacement and one of the world’s most severe humanitarian emergencies. According to Reuters, more than 14 million people have been displaced by the fighting. The war has also complicated relations with Sudan’s neighbors, particularly as rival parties accuse regional governments of providing military assistance or allowing armed groups to operate across borders. The regional security implications have become increasingly serious as Sudan’s conflict intersects with diplomatic rivalries involving Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt. Military movements near the Ethiopia-Sudan border and competing allegations of foreign support have added to concerns about wider instability. Eritrea has also accused Ethiopia of supporting Sudan’s RSF and destabilizing the Horn of Africa. Addis Ababa has denied supporting the paramilitary group, and the allegations have not been independently verified. In Ethiopia, the renewed confrontation involving federal forces and TPLF-aligned forces has raised fresh concerns about the durability of the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement, which ended the major phase of the earlier Tigray war. The security situation in northern Ethiopia remains fragile. In October, reported drone strikes near Adigrat were followed by accounts of Eritrean troop movements, illustrating how the renewed conflict has affected relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Sudanese presidential adviser Amjad Farid said Khartoum was seeking to avoid an open war with Ethiopia despite the worsening diplomatic situation. Speaking to Reuters, Farid said Sudan remained committed to defending its territory while making efforts to prevent a direct military confrontation. The departure order for the six Sudanese consular staff members adds another layer of uncertainty to relations between Addis Ababa and Khartoum. It remains unclear whether the measure will lead to further diplomatic restrictions, reciprocal expulsions or renewed negotiations between the two governments. With Sudan’s civil war continuing and security tensions rising across northern and western Ethiopia, the latest dispute underscores the risk that unresolved regional disagreements could further undermine stability across the Horn of Africa. Published 2 hours ago on November 4, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk The US Department of Justice headquarters in Washington, D.C. The department announced that Abraham Teklu Lemma pleaded guilty to transmitting classified intelligence to Ethiopian officials. Credit: APK / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 4.0 An Ethiopian-born American citizen who previously worked as a US government contractor has pleaded guilty to providing highly classified American intelligence to Ethiopian officials during a period that overlapped with the Tigray war, according to the US Department of Justice. Abraham Teklu Lemma, a Maryland resident who held a Top Secret security clearance, admitted on November 3, 2026, to conspiring to transmit US national defense information to the Ethiopian government. Prosecutors said the intelligence concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia and was supplied to senior officials within the country’s political, military and intelligence institutions. In an official announcement , the Justice Department said Lemma worked as an information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the US Department of State and the Department of Justice. According to court documents, Lemma collected and transmitted dozens of highly classified documents, notes, photographs and other materials between 2021 and his arrest in August 2023. Some of the information carried the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information classification, one of the highest levels of protection applied to US national security intelligence. Prosecutors said Lemma used his access as an IT administrator to retrieve classified information from government systems. He also copied sensitive information into handwritten notes and secretly carried them outside secure facilities. The Justice Department said these activities enabled him to pass restricted intelligence to Ethiopian government officials over an extended period. The case has drawn particular attention because the alleged espionage activities coincided with Ethiopia’s devastating northern conflict, which began in November 2020 and involved federal forces, TPLF-aligned forces and other armed actors. Although US authorities did not explicitly identify the conflict as the Tigray war in their November 3 announcement, the period covered by Lemma’s activities substantially overlaps with the fighting and its aftermath. The AFP report published on November 4 also noted the connection between the timeline of the intelligence disclosures and the conflict involving Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). US prosecutors said Lemma went beyond transmitting intelligence and, on some occasions, encouraged Ethiopian officials to take direct military action against armed groups opposing the federal government. In one exchange dated December 18, 2021, Lemma reportedly told an Ethiopian official that the opposing fighters had to be defeated to achieve peace. Later that day, according to the Justice Department, he transmitted additional information and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].” The reference to drones is particularly significant because unmanned aircraft were used during Ethiopia’s northern conflict. However, the department did not identify a specific drone operation resulting from that communication or publicly establish that a particular attack was carried out because of Lemma’s message. US officials also said the intelligence he provided was used in military operations. Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, stated that Ethiopian officials used classified national defense information supplied by Lemma during the conflict. Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said Lemma had exploited his privileged access to remove sensitive information from secure facilities and transmit it to Ethiopian officials in the hope that it would help them target and kill opposing fighters. The department’s statements establish the US government’s account of the espionage and its military implications, but they do not publicly identify specific individuals killed, military targets attacked or operations directly attributable to the leaked information. Lemma’s guilty plea marks a major development in a case that began with his arrest in August 2023. He initially faced espionage-related charges after investigators accused him of unlawfully accessing and transferring classified US government information. Under the plea agreement announced on November 3, Lemma admitted to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government, an offense under US federal law. The agreement provides for a prison sentence ranging from 120 to 262 months, equivalent to 10 years to 21 years and 10 months, subject to acceptance by the court. US District Judge John D. Bates has scheduled sentencing for April 14, 2027, in Washington, D.C. The investigation was conducted by the FBI’s Washington Field Office, with prosecutors from the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia and the Justice Department’s National Security Division handling the case. The guilty plea also raises broader questions about the handling of classified American intelligence during Ethiopia’s conflict and the role of foreign intelligence information in military decision-making. For Ethiopia, the case brings renewed international attention to the 2020–2022 northern war and the relationship between Ethiopian government officials and individuals with access to sensitive US security information. The November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement formally ended major hostilities between Ethiopia’s federal government and the TPLF , although disputes over implementation and security arrangements have continued. The US authorities’ latest announcement does not identify the Ethiopian officials who received Lemma’s information or indicate whether any of them face criminal proceedings. Lemma remains awaiting sentencing, with the court expected to determine his punishment in April 2027. Continue Reading Ethiopia Ethiopian Opposition Alliance Calls for United Action Against Abiy Government Ethiopian opposition coalition renews its political demands and appeals for cooperation. Published 4 days ago on November 1, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk A speaker reads a statement alongside two other men during an apparent Alliance for Survival press briefing. Photo credit: TMC/ Screenshot & Illustrated by Kulu Media The Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, a coalition of armed and political opposition groups, has issued a new statement calling for coordinated action against Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and outlining its position on Ethiopia’s political and security crises. In a four-page statement dated October 31, 2026, and shared on Facebook , the coalition, also known as the Alliance for Survival, accused the federal government of deepening the country’s political divisions, prolonging armed conflicts and failing to protect civilians. The alliance argued that Ethiopia’s current challenges require fundamental political change rather than measures undertaken by the existing administration. It presented cooperation among opposition organizations and communities as central to achieving that objective. The statement blamed the government for what the coalition described as widespread insecurity, displacement, human rights violations and deteriorating economic conditions. These allegations represent the alliance’s position and have not all been independently verified. The coalition also reiterated its opposition to the current federal administration and emphasized the need for a political arrangement that would protect the rights, security and participation of Ethiopia’s different communities. Its statement called for broader cooperation among political organizations, community representatives and other groups opposed to the government. It also addressed members of Ethiopia’s security institutions, urging them to reconsider their role in the country’s political and military conflicts. The alliance has previously identified the replacement of the current government and the establishment of an inclusive transitional administration as central objectives. The latest declaration continues that political position, although it does not establish that a transition has been agreed upon or that the coalition has secured additional territory or military support. The Alliance for Survival emerged in September 2026 as a coalition bringing together organizations with different political backgrounds and regional interests, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army. Its formation drew attention because some participating organizations have historically pursued competing political objectives or fought on opposing sides of earlier conflicts. Their cooperation reflects a shared opposition to the federal government, but does not necessarily mean that their wider political differences have been resolved. The new statement comes amid renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia, including confrontations involving TPLF-aligned forces, the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) and the Tigray Peace Force (TPF). Recent developments in Tigray have included the reported reentry of TPLF forces into Rama , followed by reports of drone strike damage in the area . The conflict has raised questions about the alliance’s military coordination and the extent to which its members can pursue a common strategy despite their differing political priorities. The declaration appears intended to reaffirm the coalition’s continued political cooperation and appeal for wider support. However, the statement does not independently establish a new joint military offensive, a formal agreement with additional organizations or a change in the balance of forces on the ground. No new response from the Ethiopian federal government to the October 31 statement had been independently verified at the time of writing. The alliance’s declaration adds to the political uncertainty surrounding Ethiopia’s continuing conflicts, although the practical implications of its latest calls remain unclear. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia has expelled six Sudanese diplomats amid escalating tensions between the two countries, particularly concerning allegations involving Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia. The Ethiopian government ordered the diplomats, stationed at the Sudanese consulate in Assosa, to leave within 48 hours, although no specific reason was provided for the expulsion. This diplomatic rift comes as both nations accuse each other of involvement in armed conflicts affecting the Horn of Africa. Sudan has claimed that Ethiopia allows the RSF to launch drone attacks from its territory, while Ethiopia denies these allegations. The situation is further complicated by ongoing conflicts in Sudan and northern Ethiopia, raising concerns about regional stability. The expulsion of the Sudanese diplomats could hinder diplomatic engagement, and the broader implications of these tensions may affect security and relations in the region, particularly with neighboring countries like Eritrea and Egypt.

ethiopia.content: Ethiopia expels Sudanese diplomats after fresh allegations of support for RSF | WSAU News/Talk 550 AM · 99.9 FM | Wausau, Stevens Point Menu LISTEN LIVE NEWS WEATHER ON AIR PODCASTS BLOGS AGRICULTURE OBITUARIES EVENTS PHOTOS × Sign In Search NEWS WEATHER ON AIR PODCASTS BLOGS AGRICULTURE OBITUARIES EVENTS PHOTOS Ethiopia expels Sudanese diplomats after fresh allegations of support for RSF By Thomson Reuters Nov 4, 2026 | 5:43 AM Nov 4 (Reuters) – Ethiopia has ordered six Sudanese diplomats to leave the country, a senior Ethiopian official said on Wednesday, marking a further deterioration in relations between the ​two sides over allegations each is supporting the other’s ‌enemies. Sudan accuses Ethiopia of supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, while Ethiopia accuses Sudan of backing rebels in its northern Tigray region. The allegations and counter-allegations, which both sides deny, have raised fears that the two wars could bleed ‌into ​each other, spawning a broader conflict in ⁠the Horn of Africa. On Sunday, ⁠Sudan’s government said it had lodged a complaint against Ethiopia with the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council, accusing Ethiopia of allowing the RSF ​to use its territory to launch suicide drones against civilian infrastructure in Sudan. The spokesperson for the Ethiopian prime minister’s office ⁠did not immediately respond to a ⁠Reuters request for comment. Ethiopia ordered six staff members of ​the Sudanese consulate in the border town of Assosa to leave within ​48 hours, the senior Ethiopian official said, without providing ‌a reason for the decision. The official asked not to be named to discuss a sensitive diplomatic matter. Addis Ababa denies it supports the RSF in Sudan’s civil war. The conflict has displaced more ⁠than 14 million people, according to UN figures, and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises since it erupted in April 2023. Ethiopia has ⁠accused Sudan, Egypt ‌and Eritrea of supporting Tigrayan rebels who launched ⁠an offensive against government forces in September. ​All three ‌countries have denied this. “The Sudanese government remains committed ​to its ⁠right to defend its territory. Nevertheless, it is making every possible effort to avoid an open war with Ethiopia,” Amjad Farid, political and foreign affairs adviser for Sudan’s Transitional Sovereign Council, said. ethiopia.title: The Red Sea Chokehold: Why Maritime Access Is an Existential Question for Ethiopia - horn review
ethiopia.content: The Red Sea Chokehold: Why Maritime Access Is an Existential Question for Ethiopia – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-11-04 The Red Sea Chokehold: Why Maritime Access Is an Existential Question for Ethiopia 0 Comments For a landlocked nation, maritime access is rarely a matter of simple commerce; it is an existential variable that dictates economic survival, sovereign autonomy, and strategic viability. When a country’s geographic bottleneck is policed by a deeply militarized dictator with no clear economic vision, the resulting friction transcends ordinary bilateral disputes, elevating infrastructure into a primary casus belli. No regional dynamic illustrates this geopolitical chokehold more acutely than the volatile relationship between Ethiopia and Eritrea. For decades, international observers have viewed Ethiopia’s quest for a seaport through a purely commercial lens, equating it as a matter of trade balances, shipping tariffs, and economic optimization. But as the Red Sea rapidly transforms into one of the most volatile, hyper-militarized maritime corridors on the planet, this perspective is dangerously obsolete. For Ethiopia, a nation of over 130 million people, permanent and reliable access to the sea is no longer just an economic aspiration. It is an existential imperative for national security and survival. This assertion makes sense if viewed critically beyond a shallow attempt to reduce the looming danger to a simple expansionist ambition. One must always reconsider the facts on the ground while analyzing the conundrum in the Horn of Africa. Ethiopia, a country that is only 60 kms from the Red sea, is the most populous landlocked country in the world, whose significant portion of the population is youth and in active pursuit of job opportunities. According to recent IMF reports, the country is also home to the fastest growing economy in the entire sub-Saharan Africa. This is not merely a statistical trivia point framed for political purpose; rather it is a profound strategic vulnerability. Every piece of medicine, fuel, and technology that enters the country, and every single product exported to sustain its economy, depends entirely on the political whims and stability of its coastal neighbors. Currently, Ethiopia relies on Djibouti for roughly 95% of its trade, paying upwards between $1.5 to $2 billion annually in port fees. This single door dependency is an economic chokehold. No sovereign state can safely anchor its future on a single corridor that is vulnerable to external influences. For countries like Ethiopia, the highly volatile security situation in its surrounding doubles down the impact, without mentioning the challenges associated with the growing number of military bases in the region. Should political instability or hostile foreign influence freeze the docks of Djibouti, the Ethiopian economy would collapse triggering an internal humanitarian catastrophe of unprecedented scale. This is what makes Ethiopia’s concern undeniably legitimate and fuels its determination to address what it perceives as an existential threat through any means available. Just as a drowning person instinctively tries every possible option to stay afloat. A nation of 130 million people cannot be trapped in a geographic cage at the mercy of volatile, highly militarized autocratic coastal regime. A stable, secure Horn of Africa is impossible if its largest engine of population and economic powerhouse is kept in a state of permanent anxiety and artificial suffocation. Securing a permanent and dependable commercial and naval gateway to the Red Sea is not an empire building ambition or a luxury. For Ethiopia, it is becoming a simple, legitimate right to breath and it is the only way to bring peace and security in the entire Horn. Encirclement, Exclusion, and Ethiopia’s Security Imperative The urgency underpinning Ethiopia’s vulnerability has been sharply accelerated by the growing securitization of the Red Sea. What was once an open global trade route has become an arena for geopolitical chess, dominated by state coalitions and non-state actors from near and afar. Global and regional powers increasingly framing the vital corridor as a critical national security priority rather than just a commercial shipping lane. Driven by the need to safeguard chokepoints like the Bab el Mandab Strait from asymmetric threats, piracy, and regional conflicts, world powers have rapidly expanded their footprint through a dense concentration of military bases along the coastline. Djibouti has become the primary epicenter of this militarization, uniquely hosting overlapping naval facilities for both the United States (Camp Lemonnier) and China, alongside presence from France and Japan. Concurrently, nations like Russia have sought access, while regional actors such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Turkye, and Israel are all vying for influence via port logistics and security pacts along the broader Horn of Africa. While these external militaries provide short-term protection for international shipping, their crowding presence has ultimately transformed the Red Sea into a complex arena of overlapping geopolitical rivalries and proxy vulnerabilities, weakening the prospects for a self-sustaining regional security framework and brutally doubling down on Ethiopia’s unique vulnerability. As if these threats are not enough, Ethiopia is alarmed by a recent development of an architectural web of alliances orchestrated explicitly to isolate it from its own geographic backyard. The creation of the El Alamein Joint Declaration by Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia is not as a routine diplomatic pact, but a deliberate strategy of encirclement. By codifying that Red Sea governance belongs exclusively to coastal states, regional adversaries seek to permanently deny landlocked Ethiopia a seat at the table. Proofing that the danger felt by Ethiopia is eminent beyond perception and this could potentially leave the country to consider every option to break the chokehold before it is too late. The action Ethiopia should take would be determined based on the scale and level of threats the country is faced with, as the end justifies the means. This encirclement is amplified by Egypt’s aggressive forward deployment rhetoric in the region. Driven by tensions over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), Cairo is trying to weaponize Ethiopia’s landlocked status by forming tight military and logistical alliances with Eritrea and other states bordering Ethiopia. From the Ethiopian perspective, it is quite clear. Hostile foreign militaries are aspiring to setting up base camps right on its borders, holding the keys to the very maritime gates that feed the Ethiopian population. This is a recuring dangerous move. Previously, when multinational coalitions form to protect Red Sea shipping lines from asymmetric threats like piracy and militant groups, Ethiopia is routinely excluded. Addis Ababa is being forced to watch from the sidelines while its primary economic lifeblood is policed by an alliance sympathetic to its rivals. It is profoundly naïve to expect Ethiopia to remain passive while such a perilous scheme is being orchestrated to threaten the lives of its entire population and its very survival. This reality underscores Ethiopia’s existential need to secure a reliable maritime corridor through which it can establish dependable port services and maintain a sovereign naval capability. Such a capability is essential to safeguard its national interests, protect its flag-bearing vessels, and guarantee its unhindered right to innocent passage under international law. Ethiopia has consistently expressed its preference for cooperation and has repeatedly advanced frameworks centered on mutual economic integration, shared prosperity, and regional interdependence. However, while Ethiopia remains committed to peaceful collaboration, coastal states, particularly Eritrea, should recognize that legal technicalities or strategies aimed at regional containment cannot serve as sustainable solutions to a matter that directly concerns the livelihood, security, and future of such burgeoning population. When the survival and long-term interests of the entire nation is at stake, it is unrealistic to expect Ethiopia to remain passive. It will undoubtedly pursue all the necessary strategic measures to secure its legitimate access to the Red Sea and protect its vital national interests. In doing so, it will ensure that its sovereignty, security, and economic future are safeguarded both on land and at sea. In conclusion, Ethiopia’s demand for access to the sea must be understood by its neighbouring countries as a legitimate strategic and economic and security concerns that deserves serious, constructive, and peaceful consideration. Why would Ethiopia’s quest to establish a military base along the Red Sea coast be considered unacceptable when countries from far beyond the region already maintain military bases and enjoy strategic access to the same coastline? Is it just to deny a neighbouring country with vital security and economic interests in the region an opportunity to negotiate such access, while external powers are permitted to establish a military presence there? The issue should not be approached through double standards or geopolitical rivalries, but through constructive dialogue, mutual respect, and negotiated arrangements that uphold the sovereignty of coastal states while addressing Ethiopia’s legitimate interests. IGAD and the African Union must urgently take their leadership responsibilities by facilitating inclusive regional dialogue and developing a practical framework that addresses Ethiopia’s legitimate aspirations while safeguarding the legitimate interests of neighbouring states. External actors outside the Horn of Africa should be discouraged from pursuing their agendas by fostering hostility and division, rather than promoting cooperation, dialogue, and regional stability. The international community, including the United Nations and other influential partners, should also intensify diplomatic engagement and support a negotiated settlement before the situation deteriorates into a dangerous confrontation with far reaching consequences for the Horn of Africa and beyond. The time to act is now: through timely diplomacy, mutual understanding, and political courage, regional leaders and international stakeholders can transform a potential source of conflict into an opportunity for cooperation, shared prosperity, and lasting peace. Failure to act decisively today risks allowing tensions to spiral into a devastating conflict that the region and the wider world can ill afford. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's quest for maritime access is a critical issue, transcending mere economic considerations to encompass national security and survival. As the most populous landlocked nation, Ethiopia relies heavily on Djibouti for 95% of its trade, making it vulnerable to external political influences and potential economic collapse. The Red Sea has become a militarized zone, with various global powers establishing military bases, complicating Ethiopia's situation further. Recent alliances among Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia aim to isolate Ethiopia, denying it a voice in regional maritime governance. This encirclement, coupled with tensions over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, exacerbates Ethiopia's fears of being cut off from essential resources. The country views securing a reliable maritime corridor as a legitimate right, essential for its sovereignty and economic future. Ethiopia advocates for cooperative regional dialogue to address its concerns while emphasizing the need for international support to prevent escalating tensions into conflict.

ethiopia.content: Africa Urged to Strengthen Regional Power Integration for Energy Security - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa Urged to Strengthen Regional Power Integration for Energy Security 3 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Stronger regional electricity networks and effective power markets would enable African countries to utilize their energy resources more efficiently while improving the resilience of their electricity systems, United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA) Executive Secretary Claver Gatete said today. The Executive Secretary made the call while speaking at the 36th African Hydro Symposium in Addis Ababa. According to him, energy security is increasingly a regional undertaking, requiring coordinated infrastructure planning and sustained cooperation among governments, utilities, regulators and regional organizations. Gatete further stressed that regional energy integration depends on climate-resilient hydropower development, calling for climate risk assessments, sustainable water management and stronger cooperation among countries sharing river basins. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines He also highlighted the need to improve hydropower project financing and strengthen African technical and institutional capacity to support sustainable energy development. Echoing the call for stronger regional energy integration, Water and Energy State Minister Dinku Seyum said that Ethiopia views the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) and its broader hydropower portfolio as catalysts for regional energy integration. He said surplus clean electricity from Ethiopia's hydropower resources would support cross-border power trade and foster more interconnected regional energy systems. The State Minister noted that the GERD demonstrates Ethiopia's commitment to harnessing its natural resources for sustainable development, ensuring domestic energy security while contributing to broader regional connectivity. Dinku called on African countries to strengthen cooperation in developing their hydropower resources and mobilize their own resources to overcome financing and technical capacity constraints. Ethiopia's Green Legacy Initiative and integrated watershed management efforts are important measures for protecting the environment and sustaining hydropower resources, he added, underscoring the need to diversify energy sources to strengthen climate resilience. The opening of the symposium has also seen the launch of African Union's Continental Energy Security Policy Framework which provides a common basis for advancing energy security at national and regional levels. ethiopia.summary: At the 36th African Hydro Symposium in Addis Ababa, UNECA Executive Secretary Claver Gatete emphasized the need for stronger regional electricity networks to enhance energy security across Africa. He highlighted that coordinated infrastructure planning and collaboration among governments, utilities, and regulators are essential for effective energy integration. Gatete pointed out that climate-resilient hydropower development is crucial, advocating for climate risk assessments and sustainable water management among countries sharing river basins. Ethiopian Water and Energy State Minister Dinku Seyum echoed these sentiments, noting that Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) could serve as a catalyst for regional energy integration and cross-border power trade. He urged African nations to cooperate in developing hydropower resources while addressing financing and technical capacity challenges. The symposium also launched the African Union's Continental Energy Security Policy Framework, aimed at advancing energy security at both national and regional levels, underscoring the importance of sustainable hydropower development for the continent's energy future. ethiopia.title: Abraham Teklu Lemma: US contractor gave Ethiopia secrets to help kill Tigray fighters - BBC
ethiopia.content: Abraham Teklu Lemma: US contractor gave Ethiopia secrets to help kill Tigray fighters Skip to content Watch Live British Broadcasting Corporation Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live US contractor gave Ethiopia secrets to help kill Tigray fighters 4 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Wycliffe Muia AFP via Getty Images The devastating two-year civil war killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions An Ethiopian-born American citizen has pleaded guilty to passing highly classified intelligence to Ethiopia, including information he hoped would help target and kill fighters from the Tigray region during the country's 2020-22 civil war. Abraham Teklu Lemma, a former US contractor, admitted sharing dozens of classified documents and photographs with senior Ethiopian officials over more than two years, the US Department of Justice said. "In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security," said US Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Ferris Pirro. The 54-year-old faces up to 22 years in prison under a plea agreement. Abraham had worked as a contractor at the State Department, Justice Department and National Reconnaissance Office, the agency responsible for US intelligence satellites. Prosecutors said Abraham worked with senior figures in Ethiopia's political, military and intelligence establishments between 2021 and his arrest in August 2023. He secretly removed classified material from secure government facilities, sometimes copying sensitive information into handwritten notes that he carried out of the buildings. He used his position as an IT administrator to extract electronic intelligence files. "Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia," prosecutors said. The information included satellite imagery and details of military activities, which he passed to Ethiopian officials through encrypted messages. The FBI said Ethiopian officials subsequently used intelligence supplied by Abraham in military operations. Prosecutors said he hoped the information would help Ethiopia's military identify and kill paramilitary fighters. "Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree," said John Eisenberg, the US assistant attorney general for national security. In one message to an Ethiopian official in December 2021, he wrote: "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia," court papers showed. Later that day, he shared further intelligence and urged the official: "Please send Dro[nes]." The BBC has contacted the Ethiopian authorities for comment. The revelations shed light on how sensitive American intelligence was passed to Ethiopian authorities during a devastating civil war that killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions. It was marked by widespread allegations of atrocities, including massacres, sexual violence and attacks on civilians. A peace agreement signed in November 2022 ended the conflict, although fighting resumed in September after both sides accused each other of not respecting the terms of that deal. How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia Abraham was arrested in Maryland in August 2023 following an investigation into his handling of classified intelligence. At the time, prosecutors alleged that he had removed security markings from intelligence reports and shared information with a foreign intelligence official. In one exchange, the official asked him to continue providing assistance, to which Abraham replied: "Roger that!" Pirro, the US attorney, said Abraham had abused his access to some of America's most sensitive intelligence. She accused him of betraying his colleagues and country with prosecutors saying he "will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law". Abraham pleaded guilty to conspiring to transmit national defence information to a foreign government. His sentencing is scheduled for 14 April 2027. ethiopia.summary: Abraham Teklu Lemma, an Ethiopian-born American citizen and former US contractor, has pleaded guilty to sharing classified intelligence with Ethiopian officials during the country's civil war from 2020 to 2022. He admitted to passing sensitive documents and photographs, including satellite imagery and military activity details, which he hoped would assist in targeting Tigray fighters. Lemma, who worked for various US government agencies, used his position to extract classified materials and communicate with Ethiopian officials through encrypted messages. His actions were described as a severe betrayal of his country and colleagues, jeopardizing national security. Facing up to 22 years in prison, Lemma's sentencing is scheduled for April 2027. The case highlights the significant risks associated with the unauthorized transfer of sensitive intelligence, particularly during a conflict that resulted in widespread atrocities and loss of life. The FBI noted that the intelligence he provided was utilized in military operations against Tigray fighters.

ethiopia.title: Death of Three, Injuries of 20 Kenyans Attributed to Ethiopia's Moyale Conflict
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Death of Three, Injuries of 20 Kenyans Attributed to Ethiopia's Moyale Conflict - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Death of Three, Injuries of 20 Kenyans Attributed to Ethiopia's Moyale Conflict 4 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — A Kenyan woman was killed by a suspected stray bullet in the border town of Moyale on 2 November, bringing to three the reported number of Kenyans killed in conflict linked to ongoing clashes in Moyale of neighbouring Ethiopia , according to Kenyan media reports. Amina Guchi was speaking with a security official at the Marsabit County offices near Moyale Law Courts when an object believed to be a stray bullet struck her in the back of the head. She collapsed and was rushed to Moyale Sub-County Referral Hospital, where she was pronounced dead on arrival. Police conducted a post-mortem examination before releasing her body to her family. Kenyan outlets reported that authorities linked the projectile to fighting across the border. The wider spillover has reportedly left about 20 people injured, with additional incidents involving stray bullets and rocket-propelled grenades landing on Kenyan territory. Unexploded ordnance was safely detonated near Sessi Primary School and other locations. The insecurity has disrupted education, prompting the relocation of candidates sitting the Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education examinations from schools near the border. Residents have also reported hearing gunfire from the Kenyan side. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The violence has triggered a major displacement crisis, with UN estimating that more 50,000 Ethiopians have crossed into Kenya, particularly into Marsabit County. The clashes in Ethiopian Moyale, administered by both the Oromia and Somali regional states, stem from a dispute over the establishment of a Somali Regional State administrative office and the raising of its flag in territory also claimed by Oromia. Tensions escalated following the 18 October killing of 13-year-old Diqqoo Jaataan Aagaa in an exchange of gunfire linked to the dispute. Sustained clashes involving security forces from the two regional administrations began around 22 October, with heavy weapons reportedly used as fighting spread across several districts. The conflict has caused civilian casualties, damaged homes and businesses, disrupted services and displaced tens of thousands. Independent casualty figures remain unavailable, while the continued fighting has heightened security and humanitarian concerns on both sides of the border. ethiopia.summary: The ongoing conflict in Ethiopia's Moyale has resulted in the deaths of three Kenyans and injuries to at least 20 others. A Kenyan woman, Amina Guchi, was killed by a suspected stray bullet while speaking with a security official on November 2. This incident is linked to clashes in Moyale, which have escalated since October 22, following a dispute over administrative control between the Oromia and Somali regional states. The violence has led to significant civilian casualties, damage to property, and a humanitarian crisis, with over 50,000 Ethiopians reportedly fleeing to Kenya. The conflict has disrupted education, forcing the relocation of students taking the Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education exams. Residents have reported hearing gunfire, and authorities have dealt with stray bullets and unexploded ordnance in the area. The situation remains tense, raising security and humanitarian concerns for both countries.

ethiopia.title: Rights Commission Confirms 48 Killed in Shirka Attacks, Raises Alarm Over Informal Armed Groups
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Rights Commission Confirms 48 Killed in Shirka Attacks, Raises Alarm Over Informal Armed Groups - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Rights Commission Confirms 48 Killed in Shirka Attacks, Raises Alarm Over Informal Armed Groups 4 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — The Ethiopian Human Rights Commission (EHRC) has confirmed that 48 people were killed in attacks in Shirka Woreda, Southeast Oromia, on 24 October, corroborating the death toll Addis Standard reported on 26 October based on eyewitness accounts and residents who attended the victims' mass funeral. The Commission also raised concerns over the widespread presence of informal armed groups in the area and called on authorities to strengthen civilian protection and prevent further attacks. In a statement issued following an investigation, the Rights Commission said the attack in Birbona Chole Kebele resulted in deaths, injuries, the destruction of homes and the displacement of hundreds of residents. It said the findings were established through interviews with victims, families of the deceased, eyewitnesses, community representatives, religious leaders, medical personnel and government officials, alongside field observations and digital investigative techniques. According to the Commission, an armed group identifying itself as the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), commonly referred to as "Shane" or OLF-Shane, entered Birbona Chole Kebele from four directions between 12:30 a.m. and 2:30 a.m. on 24 October. The attack killed 23 locally organized security personnel, five militia members and 13 civilians. The Commission separately confirmed that seven additional civilians were killed by informal armed individuals operating in the area. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The attacks also left 20 people injured, while 21 residential houses were burned and 247 families displaced. An undetermined number of cattle and pack animals were also looted, the Commission said. The findings corroborate Addis Standard's earlier reporting on the scale of the killings. On 26 October, residents who attended the victims' mass funeral told Addis Standard that at least 48 people had been killed and more than 31 others wounded in attacks in Chole and Birbo kebeles. Witnesses described door-to-door killings, looting and the use of heavy weapons, saying the victims included women, elderly people and at least six children under the age of 15. The latest findings also come amid government security operations following the killings. On 2 November, Addis Standard reported that the Oromia regional government had announced the detention of 73 individuals in connection with the attacks, describing the arrests as part of operations against OLF-Shane and other groups it considers security threats. The regional government said security had been restored in six kebeles and that assistance was being provided to displaced residents to facilitate their return. Recurring attacks and civilian protection concerns Beyond confirming the death toll, the Rights Commission's investigation highlighted the broader security challenges in the area, particularly the presence of informal armed individuals operating outside formal government security structures. Chief Commissioner Birhanu Adelo described the killings, injuries, property destruction and displacement as deeply concerning, urging the government to provide adequate and effective protection in affected communities and other areas facing similar security threats. He called on authorities to review local security arrangements, strengthen early-warning systems and respond promptly to emerging threats. He also stressed the need for a swift, independent and effective investigation to establish accountability, provide assistance to victims and families of those killed, facilitate the safe return of displaced residents, and ensure compensation and rehabilitation. The Commission recalled that it had repeatedly urged the government to address recurring attacks in Aseko, Anqolo Wabe, Guna and Merti woredas in the former Arsi Zone, warning that sustainable preventive measures were necessary to protect civilians and prevent further violations. Citing Article 13(1) of Ethiopia's Constitution, the Commission stressed that federal and regional government institutions have an obligation to respect, protect and fulfil the rights to life, property, personal security and liberty. It said authorities must go beyond investigating violations and holding perpetrators accountable to address the underlying causes of insecurity, including through effective oversight of informal armed groups. This figure aligns with earlier reports based on eyewitness accounts. The attacks, attributed to an armed group known as the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), resulted in significant casualties, including 23 security personnel, five militia members, and 13 civilians, alongside injuries to 20 others. The violence also led to the destruction of homes and the displacement of 247 families. The EHRC expressed alarm over the prevalence of informal armed groups and urged the government to enhance civilian protection and address security challenges. The Commission called for a thorough investigation into the incidents and emphasized the need for effective measures to prevent future attacks. In response to the violence, the Oromia regional government has detained 73 individuals linked to the attacks and is providing assistance to displaced residents.

somalia.title: Somalia Says Uganda's Troop Withdrawal Does Not Mean All Forces Are Leaving - Garowe Online
somalia.content: Somalia Says Uganda's Troop Withdrawal Does Not Mean All Forces Are Leaving Latest Headlines Somalia Says Uganda's Troop Withdrawal Does Not Mean All Forces Are Leaving Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race, becomes first Muslim elected to US Senate From the Battlefields to the Classrooms — Al-Baraa bin Malik Brigade’s Next-Generation Strategy Somalia: Puntland Health Minister Pledges World-Class Hospital to Expand Medical Services Indian airborne commandos recapture ship off Somalia Advertise with us Home News Puntland Somalia World Sports Press Releases Somaliland Videos Opinion Contact Privacy Policy English Somali Somalia Says Uganda's Troop Withdrawal Does Not Mean All Forces Are Leaving Staff Reporter GAROWE ONLINE Posted On 04-11-2026, 01:57PM MOGADISHU, Somalia — Somalia's federal government has clarified that the withdrawal of Ugandan troops deployed under a bilateral agreement does not mean all Ugandan forces are leaving the country. Somalia's National Security Adviser, Ambassador Aweys Haji Yusuf Ahmed, said the troops currently being withdrawn are mainly those deployed under a separate agreement between the governments of Somalia and Uganda. He stressed that Ugandan forces serving under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) remain in the country and will continue their duties alongside other mission contingents and the Somali National Army. "The withdrawal of troops deployed under bilateral agreements should not be interpreted as the departure of all Ugandan forces from Somalia," Aweys said. His remarks followed an announcement by the Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) that it had begun withdrawing troops deployed in Somalia under bilateral arrangements, with the first contingent already returning to Uganda. In a statement issued Nov. 2, the UPDF said the withdrawal of those troops would be completed within days. It added that all Ugandan forces in Somalia, including those serving under AUSSOM, are expected to leave by the end of 2027. Aweys made the clarification after chairing a tripartite meeting involving the Somali federal government, AUSSOM and the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS). The meeting reaffirmed the three parties' commitment to strengthening their coordination framework to improve cooperation, strategic planning and logistical support for AUSSOM and the Somali National Army. Participants also stressed the need for sustained, predictable and adequate international support to accelerate Somalia's security transition, consolidate gains from ongoing military operations and strengthen the operational capabilities of the country's security forces. The withdrawal announcement comes as Somalia continues to rely on international support to sustain security operations against al-Shabab militants and strengthen its national forces. somalia.content: Somalia, Djibouti sign agreement to strengthen parliamentary cooperation - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia, Djibouti sign agreement to strengthen parliamentary cooperation Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday November 3, 2026 Djibouti City (HOL) – Somalia and Djibouti have signed a memorandum of understanding to strengthen cooperation between their parliaments, focusing on legislative development, institutional capacity-building and the exchange of expertise. The agreement was signed on Monday in Djibouti City by the Speaker of Somalia’s House of the People and the Speaker of Djibouti’s National Assembly, Dileita Mohamed Dileita. Under the agreement, the two parliaments will cooperate on improving legislative procedures, training parliamentary staff, conducting legal research and modernizing their institutional operations. The memorandum also provides for closer cooperation between parliamentary standing committees, the use of modern technology, improved data security and the establishment of parliamentary friendship groups between the two countries. Both sides also agreed to coordinate their positions on issues discussed at regional and international parliamentary forums. Following the signing ceremony, Dileita welcomed the outcome of discussions with the Somali delegation, saying the exchange of views had produced positive results for both countries. The Somali parliamentary speaker said Mogadishu was committed to strengthening ties with Djibouti through knowledge-sharing and institutional cooperation. The agreement is part of broader efforts by the two neighboring countries to expand bilateral relations and strengthen cooperation between their government institutions. somalia.title: Somalia Produces Just 5% of Estimated Annual Fishery Capacity - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somalia Produces Just 5% of Estimated Annual Fishery Capacity - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia Produces Just 5% of Estimated Annual Fishery Capacity Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday November 3, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia produces about 30,000 tonnes of fish annually, just 5% of its estimated marine fishery production capacity of 600,000 tonnes, according to a report by The EastAfrican, as the country seeks to attract investment into its underdeveloped fishing industry. Abdi Dirshe, director general of Somalia's Ministry of Fisheries and Blue Economy, said the gap between current output and estimated capacity stands at nearly 570,000 tonnes a year. Dirshe estimated that the sector could generate between $1.8 billion and $3 billion in annual revenue and create more than 210,000 jobs if its resources were properly developed. The figures represent potential economic returns rather than existing industry revenue or employment. Somalia has approximately 3,333 kilometres of coastline, but inadequate fishing equipment, limited processing and storage facilities, and security concerns have restricted the industry's development. Investment and fisheries policy Expanding production would require investment in fishing vessels, equipment, landing sites, cold storage, processing plants and export infrastructure. Abdullahi Adan, coordinator of Somalia's Sustainable Fisheries Development Project, known as Badmaal, said the government's National Transformation Plan 2025–2029 prioritises private investment, market development and public-private partnerships in the sector. Somalia has introduced legal and regulatory measures intended to encourage investment, including an Investment Law, a public-private partnership policy, a Fisheries Law and food safety regulations. Local companies have also begun investing in fish processing and boatbuilding, with projects aimed at creating jobs and developing technical skills among young Somalis. Export markets and security challenges Engineer Ali Ibrahim Siyad, chairman of the Somali Fish Exporters Association, said quality assurance and seafood certification are essential for gaining access to international markets. He identified the United States, China, the Middle East and East African countries as potential destinations for Somali fish exports. However, exporters face difficulties meeting the requirements of international markets, while the industry continues to operate with limited infrastructure and equipment. Fisheries expert Omar Abdulle Hayle said security remains the primary consideration for investors seeking to protect their personnel and assets. The report also identified limited capacity to protect marine resources as an obstacle to developing the industry. Fisheries experts called for transparent management and stronger marine environmental protection alongside efforts to increase production. somalia.summary: Somalia's fishing industry is currently underperforming, producing only 30,000 tonnes of fish annually, which is just 5% of its estimated capacity of 600,000 tonnes, according to a report by The EastAfrican. Abdi Dirshe, director general of the Ministry of Fisheries and Blue Economy, highlighted a significant gap of nearly 570,000 tonnes, suggesting that with proper development, the sector could generate between $1.8 billion and $3 billion in revenue and create over 210,000 jobs. The country, with a 3,333-kilometre coastline, faces challenges such as inadequate equipment, limited processing facilities, and security concerns that hinder industry growth. The government aims to attract private investment through its National Transformation Plan 2025–2029 and has introduced legal measures to encourage investment. However, exporters struggle with quality assurance and certification for international markets, while security remains a primary concern for potential investors. Experts emphasize the need for better management and environmental protection to enhance production. (160 words)

somalia.summary: The Somali government has condemned Israel's plans to establish an embassy in Somaliland, asserting that this move violates Somalia's sovereignty and territorial integrity. The Foreign Ministry in Mogadishu declared the decision as legally null and void, emphasizing that Hargeisa and the northwestern regions are integral parts of Somalia. Somalia warned that Israel's actions could escalate security tensions in the region and stated its intention to pursue diplomatic, political, and legal measures to protect its territorial rights. This condemnation follows Israel's recognition of Somaliland in December 2025, marking a significant diplomatic shift since Somaliland declared self-governance nearly 35 years ago. Somaliland, however, has rejected Somalia's claims, asserting its right to establish foreign relations independently, including its ties with Israel. The situation highlights the ongoing complexities of sovereignty and diplomatic recognition in the Horn of Africa.

somalia.summary: A tragic incident occurred at Dhusamareb Airport in Somalia, where Mukhtar Qasim Samay, a bodyguard for Mogadishu Police Chief Ma'alin Mahdi, was killed after walking into a spinning aircraft propeller. The accident happened on Tuesday as Samay had just disembarked from the plane. Reports indicate that the propeller struck him in the head, leading to his death. Chief Mahdi and his team had arrived at the airport to attend the inauguration of Galmudug's leadership, scheduled for Thursday. This unfortunate event highlights the dangers associated with airport operations and the need for heightened safety measures around aircraft. The incident has drawn attention to the risks faced by security personnel in high-stakes environments.

somalia.summary: The Indian Navy successfully rescued an Iranian fishing vessel, the Azini, which had been hijacked by pirates off the coast of Somalia. The operation, lasting over 48 hours, involved the coordinated efforts of a mission-deployed warship and a maritime reconnaissance aircraft. The vessel, with 20 crew members aboard, was taken by an armed group in October, posing a significant maritime security threat as it could have been used as a "mother ship" for further attacks on merchant shipping. The Indian Navy tracked the vessel's movements and employed non-kinetic measures to prevent its escape. Marine commandos were deployed via a precision airdrop from an Indian Air Force C-17 aircraft. The operation concluded with the safe rescue of all crew members, with no casualties reported. This successful intervention highlights India's commitment to being a first responder and a preferred security partner in the Indian Ocean Region. (160 words)

During the meeting, Al Omairi conveyed greetings from His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik, expressing wishes for the President's health and happiness, as well as for the stability and prosperity of the Somali people. This diplomatic engagement marks a significant step in strengthening ties between the two nations, reflecting mutual respect and cooperation.

العمومية المقررة في مارس 2027 لانتخاب مجلس إدارة جديد، حيث ستحظى الإدارة بدعم كبير إذا نجحت في استعادة كرشوم الذي قدم سنوات مميزة مع الفريق، وأسهم بفاعلية في بلوغه دور المجموعات بدوري أبطال أفريقيا 3 نسخ متتالية. وقد أثارت هذه الرغبة قلق الغريم التقليدي الهلال الذي يستعد بقوة لمرحلة المجموعات. ومن المتوقع أن يحسم اللاعب مستقبله خلال الفترة المقبلة؛ ففي حال تمديد عقده مع ناديه الحالي، ستتلاشى آمال football.summary: تسبب نادي المريخ في إرباك تحضيرات نادي الهلال السوداني لمجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا، حيث عاد نجم الهلال، مصطفى كرشوم، إلى الواجهة بعد تقديمه مستويات مميزة في التصفيات الأفريقية. يسعى المريخ لاستعادة كرشوم، الذي يعتبر من أفضل المدافعين في السودان، بينما يحاول الهلال الحفاظ عليه من خلال تمديد عقده قبل دخوله "الفترة الحرة". إدارة الهلال بدأت تحركات مبكرة لتأمين بقاء اللاعب، الذي أعاد الصلابة لدفاع الفريق بعد تذبذب مستوياته السابقة. في المقابل، إدارة المريخ تأمل في استعادة كرشوم، مما يزيد من حدة المنافسة بين الفريقين. اللاعب سيحسم مستقبله قريبًا، حيث إن تجديد عقده مع الهلال قد يقضي على آمال المريخ في ضمه، خاصة مع اقترابه من الاعتزال في سن الـ35.

اكتسح الترشيحات.. نجم الهلال السوداني يقترب من تتويج خاص لاعبو الهلال السوداني (Facebook/ Al Hilal S.C) 2 نوفمبر 2026 اكتسح الترشيحات.. نجم الهلال السوداني يقترب من تتويج خاص الهلال السوداني الدوري السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' أشعلت جماهير الهلال السوداني منافسة خاصة بين نجوم الفريق، مصطفى كرشوم وأرنست لوزولو وياسر عوض، للفوز بجائزة "أفضل لاعب في شهر أكتوبر" التي خصصتها إدارة النادي لتحفيز اللاعبين ورفع مستوى أدائهم. ويعد المدافع مصطفى كرشوم المرشح الأبرز لنيل الجائزة بفضل مستواه المتميز الذي قدمه خلال الشهر الماضي، لا سيما في مباراتي سيداما بونا الإثيوبي بالدور التمهيدي الثاني لمسابقة دوري أبطال أفريقيا، مما جعله يحظى باهتمام واسع من الجماهير، وتقدم اللاعب بوضوح مكتسحًا زميليه مقتربًا من تحقيق مكسب مهم قبل صدامات قارية مرتقبة. في المقابل، يواصل ياسر عوض حضوره القوي في المنافسة للشهر الثاني على التوالي، بعد أن كان مرشحًا بارزًا في شهر سبتمبر/ أيلول الماضي. ونجح اللاعب المحلي في قلب الطاولة على المحترف الكونغولي ستيفن إيبويلا وأزاحه عن مركز الظهير الأيمن، ليستأثر بفرصة المشاركة بصفة أساسية بعد أن كسب ثقة المدرب جوزيف زينباور. اقرأ أيضًا بعد رسائل الحزم.. مدرب الهلال يتلقى دعما قبل مواعيد حاسمة الهلال السوداني يستعيد توازنه بفوز ثمين في الدوري الرواندي بدوره، فرض أرنست لوزولو نفسه ضمن قائمة المرشحين بعد أن نجح في تسجيل هدف رائع في شباك سيداما بونا الإثيوبي، مقدمًا مستويات باهرة، ومسهمًا في تحقيق فريقه لانتصارات محلية وقارية. كرشوم يواصل تألقه مع الهلال السوداني من جانبه، يمثل مدافع الهلال السوداني مصطفى كرشوم ظاهرة نادرة في الملاعب السودانية، لاستمرار تألقه ومحافظته على مستواه مع المنتخب وفريقه، مما جعله ضمن قائمة أفضل اللاعبين في البلاد خلال السنوات الأخيرة. ورغم بلوغه سن الـ35، يتطلع اللاعب لظهورٍ لافت في الموسم الحالي، خاصة مع اقتراب دخوله الفترة الحرة، طامحًا في الحصول على تقييم يتناسب مع موهبته وخبراته، واغتنام فرصة التجديد الأخيرة قبل اعتزاله. من المتوقع أن تعلن إدارة النادي عن الفائز بالجائزة في حفلٍ مصغر دأبت على إقامته دوريًا. مع العلم أنّ المحترف الموريتاني في صفوف الفريق، أحمد سالم مبارك، كان قد توج بالجائزة عن شهر سبتمبر/ أيول الماضي وسط حفاوة كبيرة من زملائه، فيما يعد مصطفى كرشوم المرشح الأوفر حظا لنيل الجائزة عن شهر أكتوبر. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة
